metrics.title: Who pays the income tax
metrics.question: What share of all personal income tax does each income group pay?

headline.caption: of all personal income tax was paid by the top 1% of taxpayers

benchmark.label: Top 10% of taxpayers
benchmark.text: 43.7% of all personal income tax in 2023-24

metrics.status_rule: Shown for context, with no verdict. How the tax load should be shared is a political judgement.
context: In 2023-24 the top 1% of taxpayers was 132,399 people with taxable incomes of $429,531 or more. Together they paid about $55.3 billion of the $329.5 billion in personal income tax.
The top 10% paid 43.7% of all personal income tax. The middle 40% paid 43.0%, and the bottom half of taxpayers paid 13.3%.
The shares have changed little over the decade. The top 1% paid 17.0% in 2013-14 and 16.8% in 2023-24, with a high of 19.6% in 2021-22.
The ATO does not publish how many high earners leave Australia each year, or how much tax they paid before leaving.
These figures cover personal income tax only. Company tax, GST and other taxes are not included.

chart.note: Share of all net personal income tax paid by each group of taxpayers, ranked by taxable income. The 4 groups add up to 100%.

sources.title: Taxation statistics 2023-24, Individuals Table 16: Percentile distribution of taxable individuals
series: Net tax by taxable income percentile, Individuals Table 16A, editions 2013-14 to 2023-24

metrics.method: Net tax by taxable income percentile from ATO Taxation Statistics, Individuals Table 16A, for each income year from 2013-14 to 2023-24, added up across sexes and states. Percentiles rank taxable individuals by taxable income. Each group's share is its net tax divided by the net tax of all taxable individuals.

explainer.what: Everyone who paid income tax in a year, lined up from the lowest taxable income to the highest and split into groups. The chart shows what share of the total tax bill each group paid.
explainer.why: Income tax is the government's biggest source of revenue. Because the system is progressive, a small group of high earners pays a large share. Changes in who earns what, or who lives here, affect how much tax is collected and who pays it.

metrics.title: Money sent overseas by individuals
metrics.question: How much do people living in Australia send to family and friends overseas?

headline.caption: sent overseas as personal transfers in a year

metrics.status_rule: Shown for context, with no verdict. Sending money to family overseas is a private choice.
context: $2.7 billion was sent overseas as personal transfers in 2025-26, up from $1.9 billion in 2021-22 and $1.1 billion in 2013-14.
The ABS does not publish this series for money sent to people in Australia from overseas, so a net figure is not available.
The figures are not broken down by the country the money goes to or by the background of the person sending it.

chart.note: Money and goods sent by people living in Australia to people overseas, each financial year. ABS estimate.

sources.title: Balance of Payments and International Investment Position, Australia
series: Secondary income debits, Other sectors, Personal transfers, original, current prices

metrics.method: ABS Balance of Payments, secondary income debits, other sectors, personal transfers, original series at current prices. The 4 quarters of each financial year are added together and shown in billions of dollars.

explainer.what: Personal transfers are money or goods sent by people living in Australia to people overseas without anything in return, mostly to family. The ABS estimates them as part of the balance of payments.
explainer.why: They are one of the ways money leaves the country, alongside imports, overseas travel and payments to foreign investors. They tend to grow as the population and incomes grow.

metrics.title: Spending on consultants
metrics.question: How much do federal agencies commit to consultancy contracts each year?

headline.caption: in consultancy contracts starting in the year

benchmark.label: 2021-22, the year before the change of government

metrics.status_rule: Shown for context, with no verdict. There is no official target for consultancy spending.
context: Federal agencies committed $759.8 million to 2,297 consultancy contracts starting in 2025-26, against $705.0 million on 2,923 contracts in 2021-22.
The value fell to $614.8 million in 2022-23, then rose for 2 years to a high of $785.8 million in 2024-25.
In 2012-13 the figure was $371.0 million, so it has roughly doubled over 13 years.
These are the full values of the contracts, which are often paid over several years, not the amount paid out in each year.
Consultancies are only part of what agencies spend on outside help. Contractors and labour hire are counted separately and cost several times more.
The Auditor-General counted $887.7 million for 2021-22 using a different method that also counts each later change to a contract as its own entry.

series.name: Consultancy contracts starting in the year

chart.note: Total value of contracts flagged as consultancies on AusTender, by the financial year the contract starts. Current value, including any later changes. Includes GST.

sources.title: AusTender contract notices, consultancy contracts by start date
series: Contract notices with Consultancy = Yes, by contract start date, financial years 2012-13 to 2025-26

sources.title: Australian Government procurement contract reporting: 2022 update

metrics.method: Downloaded from AusTender's contract notice search with Consultancy set to Yes and the contract start date in each financial year. Each contract is counted once, at its latest value including any amendments. Values are the full contract value including GST, not annual payments. Contracts under $10,000 are not reported on AusTender. Agencies have 42 days to publish a contract, so the latest year may still rise a little.

explainer.what: A consultancy is a contract for independent expert advice, such as a review, an evaluation or a strategy, where the work reflects the consultant's own judgement. Agencies flag these contracts when they publish them on AusTender, the government's contract register. This chart adds up the value of every flagged contract by the year it starts.
explainer.why: Consultancy spending is a common test of whether the public service has the skills to do its own work. Both major parties have promised to cut it. The figures show how much is being committed, not whether the advice was good value.
